From Predictive Geometry to Action: Learning Complementary Predictive Representations for Embodied Manipulation

Xiaoxu Xu Affiliation: Beihang University Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory    Hao Li Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory    Hongtao Zhang Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory    Yili Tang Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory    Jiafei Cao Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory    Junhao Cai   Haoxiang Ma   Weixin Li   Weinan Zhang Affiliation: Beihang University Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
Abstract

Effective manipulation requires a policy to capture not only about the current scene geometry, but also about how that geometry will evolve under interaction. Existing approaches either augment policies with geometric information from current observations or introduce future prediction as auxiliary supervision, leaving open how predictive geometry should be represented for action generation. Therefore, we propose a two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations from multi-view video clips. During pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model provides dense geometric features that are compressed into predictive geometric representations and optimized to preserve scene structure and its temporal evolution. Action supervision is then applied to geometric transitions to extract a complementary motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant transitions. During downstream post-training, predictive geometry is transferred through geometry queries, while the motor representation guides intermediate features along the action-generation pathway. Future observations are used only as privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm tasks, our approach consistently improves downstream policies, including an absolute gain of 10.4 percentage points on the WidowX evaluation. We further demonstrate transfer across multiple VLA architectures and WAMs, with improvements in both future-world and action prediction. The code will be available at https://github.com/xuxiaoxxxx/CPR.

22footnotetext: †\dagger Corresponding author.

1 Introduction

Anticipating how the physical world will evolve(Assran et al., 2025; Assran et al., 2023) under interaction is becoming increasingly important for vision-language-action (VLA) models(Ma et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026) and world action models (WAM)(Li et al., 2026b; Ye et al., 2026). Such predictive capability allows an agent to reason about the consequences of interaction, rather than mapping only its current observation to an immediate action. Yet effective manipulation requires more than temporal foresight alone: it also depends on a precise understanding of how the scene is spatially organized. Geometry specifies object layouts, spatial relationships, and robot-scene configurations, while dynamics describe how these structures evolve as an interaction unfolds. For action generation, these two aspects play distinct but complementary roles: geometry provides the spatial structure within which actions are executed, while its evolution provides cues about how the scene may change over time. This naturally raises a central question: how should geometric structure and its predicted evolution be represented so that they can more effectively support action generation?

Recent efforts to incorporate geometry into predictive policy learning follow two directions. As shown in Fig.1, input-centric approaches(Sun et al., 2025; Qu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026c; Zhang et al., 2025b) augment observations with depth, point clouds, 3D coordinates, or pretrained geometric features. These methods improve spatial grounding, but use geometry as additional context for describing the currently observed scene and may rely on sensing or geometry-estimation pipelines. Prediction-centric approaches(Yang et al., 2026a; He et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025c; Su et al., 2026) instead supervise models with future RGB-D observations, future geometric states, or other world-prediction targets, explicitly exposing the policy to future scene structure. However, such targets are represented as dense observations or holistic latent states, requiring the learned representation to retain geometric information whose relevance to control may vary substantially. More broadly, these approaches primarily organize geometry to represent the scene and its evolution. They leave less explicit how action-relevant information should be distinguished from geometry needed for a coherent world representation. This creates a gap between predictive geometric modeling and action-oriented motor representation learning.

A natural way to bridge this gap is to recognize that predictive geometry and action generation place different preferences on learned representations. Predictive geometric modeling benefits from preserving a sufficiently complete and coherent account of scene structure. Action generation, in contrast, benefits from emphasizing geometric variations that are informative for motor commands while reducing the influence of static or action-irrelevant scene content. Rather than forcing these roles to be served in exactly the same representation, we introduce two complementary representations with distinct but related purposes: a predictive geometric representation that provides a compact and structured description of scene geometry and its evolution, and a motor representation that emphasizes action-aware information from geometric transitions. The former provides structured predictive context, while the latter focuses this predictive information toward control.

Building on this observation, we propose the two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations (CPR) from large-scale heterogeneous interaction videos(Collaboration, 2023; Jin et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2024; Goyal et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2025a) and transfers them to downstream policies. As illustrated in Fig. 1, our framework first constructs a predictive geometric representation from dense geometric features and then extracts action-aware information from the temporal evolution of scene geometry across video clips, providing complementary guidance for downstream action generation. Specifically, as shown in Fig.2, during representation pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model (Wang et al., 2025) extracts dense geometric features from multi-view video observations, which are progressively compressed by a hierarchical query-based encoder into compact temporal states. Geometry reconstruction, masked representation prediction, and geometric transition prediction encourage the predictive geometric representation to preserve scene structure while capturing its evolution over time. We then apply action supervision to transitions between consecutive predictive geometric states, yielding a motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant geometric transitions. The predictive geometric representation therefore captures structured information about the evolving scene, while the motor representation focuses on transitions that are more directly informative for action. During post-training, as shown in Fig.3, these two representations are transferred through role-specific supervision pathways. Dedicated geometry queries are trained to infer the predictive geometric representation from current-time inputs, while intermediate features along the action-generation pathway are aligned with the motor representation. Importantly, future observations and the pretrained representation model are used only to construct privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. We evaluate CPR on both multiple VLA architectures and WAM across diverse simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks, demonstrating consistent improvements across different robot embodiments and action-generation paradigms. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We identify complementary roles for predictive geometric and motor representations in predictive policy learning: predictive geometric modeling benefits from preserving structured scene geometry, while action generation benefits from emphasizing control-relevant geometric transitions.

  • •

    We develop a two-stage framework that learns and transfers these complementary predictive representations. Hierarchical geometric tokenization and predictive objectives learn geometric states, while action supervision extracts action-aware information from their transitions; the two representations are transferred through geometry-query and motor-alignment pathways.

  • •

    Extensive experiments across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm manipulation tasks demonstrate consistent improvements across policy architectures and robot embodiments. CPR yields a 10.4% absolute gain on the WidowX evaluation and improves future-world and action prediction in WAM.

2 Related Work

Predictive Representations for VLA and WAM.

Predictive modeling provides VLA models and WAMs with foresight beyond the current observation. Existing approaches introduce future information either through observation prediction or compact predictive representations. Observation-level methods predict future RGB observations, videos, or world states to support action generation (Zhang et al., 2025a; Lv et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026; Agarwal et al., 2026), while latent-space approaches compress future information into compact conditions or visuomotor representations (Xu et al., 2026; Su et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). Recent methods (Lee et al., 2026b; Yan et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2025b; Ding and Wang, 2026), also explore structured predictive signals such as dynamic, spatial, or semantic information to connect VLMs or world modeling with control. However, existing methods vary in how geometric structure and action-relevant temporal transitions are organized. Our work focuses specifically on predictive geometry: we learn a structured representation that preserves scene geometry and its evolution, and derive a complementary motor representation from geometric transitions.

Geometric Learning for Robotic Manipulation.

Geometric information has been increasingly incorporated into robotic policies to improve spatial grounding. Input-centric approaches (Qu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025; Bhat et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Huang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026b) augment current observations with depth, point clouds, 2D or 3D coordinates, or spatial features, providing direct access to the geometry of the observed scene. More recent prediction-centric approaches (Li et al., 2025c; He et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a; Su et al., 2026) instead use geometric or spatiotemporal prediction as auxiliary supervision, including depth prediction, robot trajectories, and 3D motion representations. These approaches demonstrate the value of geometry for predictive policy learning, but geometric structure and action relevance may favor different types of information: preserving scene geometry requires broad structural fidelity, whereas action generation benefits from transitions that are informative for motor behavior. Our work addresses this distinction by learning complementary predictive geometric and motor representations, and transferring them separately to downstream policies through dedicated interfaces.

3 Method

We present a two-stage framework for learning complementary predictive representations and transferring them to downstream policies. As illustrated in Fig. 2, during (i) Complementary Predictive Representation Pretraining, continuous multi-view video clips are first converted into compact predictive geometric representations that preserve the spatial structure of the scene while capturing its temporal evolution. We then use the transitions between these predictive geometric representations, together with temporally aligned action supervision, to extract action-aware information into a complementary motor representation. During (ii) Representation-Guided Policy Post-training, as shown in Fig.3, the predictive geometric representations and motor representations are transferred to the policy through two dedicated supervision pathways. Geometry queries are trained to infer structured predictive geometric information from current-time inputs, while intermediate features along the action-generation pathway are aligned with the motor representation.

3.1 Complementary Predictive Representation Pretraining

Hierarchical Geometric Tokenization.

As shown in Fig.2, we first transform dense multi-view observations into a compact and temporally organized sequence of geometric states. A frozen pretrained 3D foundation model (Wang et al., 2025) is applied independently to each frame-view pair OtvO_{t}^{v}, where t∈Tt\in T and v∈Vv\in V denote the number of frames and camera views, respectively, producing dense geometric features 𝐅tv\mathbf{F}_{t}^{v}. These features provide rich spatial information, but directly modeling all geometric tokens across views and time incurs substantial computational overhead. We therefore introduce a hierarchical query-based encoder that progressively compresses the representation along the view and temporal dimensions.

At each time step tt, geometric features from all camera views are concatenated along the token dimension and augmented with learnable view embeddings to preserve view-specific information. A set of learnable geometric queries then cross-attends to the resulting multi-view tokens, producing a compact frame-level geometric state 𝐇t\mathbf{H}_{t}. We subsequently aggregate the frame-level states along the temporal dimension. Inspired by (Wan et al., 2025), the first state 𝐇0\mathbf{H}_{0} is retained without temporal aggregation and serves as a temporal anchor, while each complete group of four subsequent frame-level states is compressed into one temporal slot. This produces KK temporal slots, where K=1+⌊T−14⌋K=1+\left\lfloor\frac{T-1}{4}\right\rfloor. Temporal positional embeddings are introduced before temporal aggregation to preserve the ordering of the underlying frames. We denote the resulting tokenized geometric sequence as 𝐒={𝐒k}k=1K\mathbf{S}=\{\mathbf{S}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}. This hierarchical design substantially reduces the spatiotemporal token budget while maintaining an explicitly organized representation of scene geometry over time.

Predictive Geometric Representation Learning.

Although the tokenized geometric sequence 𝐒\mathbf{S} provides compact descriptions of individual temporal segments, each state alone does not explicitly encode how the interaction evolves over time. As shown in Fig.2, we therefore process the sequence using a causal Slot-Temporal Mixer, implemented as a stack of causal attention blocks. At temporal slot kk, the representation attends only to states at or before kk, such that each output summarizes the geometric history available up to that point. The resulting sequence forms the predictive geometric representations 𝐆={𝐆k}k=1K\mathbf{G}=\{\mathbf{G}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}.

We shape 𝐆\mathbf{G} with three complementary objectives, each emphasizing a different property of predictive geometric information. Geometry reconstruction preserves the spatial information inherited from the frozen 3D foundation model; masked geometric representation prediction encourages temporal consistency and contextual inference across geometric states; and geometric transition prediction explicitly models local transitions between consecutive states. Together, these objectives encourage 𝐆\mathbf{G} to remain structurally informative while capturing predictable patterns in the evolution of scene geometry.

1) Geometry Reconstruction. Hierarchical tokenization substantially compresses the dense geometric features and may consequently discard information about the underlying scene structure. To preserve such information, we attach a reconstruction decoder to the compact geometric pathway. The decoder mirrors the encoding hierarchy by first expanding the temporal slots into frame-level representations and subsequently reconstructing the geometric features associated with each camera view, yielding 𝐅^tv\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{t}^{v}. Let Ω\Omega denote the set of valid frame-view pairs. We optimize

ℒrec=1|Ω|​∑(t,v)∈ΩSmoothL1⁡(𝐅^tv,sg⁡(𝐅tv)),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{(t,v)\in\Omega}\operatorname{SmoothL1}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{t}^{v},\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{F}_{t}^{v})\right), (1)

where sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}(\cdot) denotes the stop-gradient operator. By reconstructing features from the frozen 3D encoder rather than raw observations, this objective encourages the compact representation to retain geometrically informative scene structure despite the substantial token compression.

2) Masked Geometric Representation Prediction. To further capture temporal dependencies among geometric states, we introduce a slot-level masked prediction objective that requires missing geometric states to be inferred from the available temporal context. Specifically, we randomly sample a subset of temporal slots ℳ⊆{2,…,K}\mathcal{M}\subseteq\{2,\ldots,K\} for masking. A full-sequence target branch processes all temporal slots through the Slot-Temporal Mixer to produce the target representation 𝐆\mathbf{G}. In parallel, a context branch processes the masked temporal slots using the same weight-shared Slot-Temporal Mixer. A lightweight predictor then uses the resulting contextual representations to estimate the target states at the masked positions, producing 𝐆^m\widehat{\mathbf{G}}_{m} for each m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M}. The objective is

ℒmask=1|ℳ|​∑m∈ℳSmoothL1⁡(𝐆^m,sg⁡(𝐆m))+λvc​ℛvc​(𝐆),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mask}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}|}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}\operatorname{SmoothL1}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{G}}_{m},\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{G}_{m})\right)+\lambda_{\mathrm{vc}}\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{vc}}(\mathbf{G}), (2)

where ℛvc\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{vc}} denotes a variance-covariance regularizer. Its variance term maintains sufficient dispersion across feature dimensions, while its covariance term discourages redundant correlations between dimensions. Together, they prevent degenerate latent solutions and promote an informative predictive state space.

3) Geometric Transition Prediction. Masked representation prediction encourages contextual inference among temporal states, but does not directly constrain the direction in which the latent geometry evolves. We therefore explicitly model local geometric transitions. For two consecutive predictive states, we define the latent transition as

Δ𝐆k=𝐆k+1−𝐆k,k=1,…,K−1,\Delta\mathbf{G}_{k}=\mathbf{G}_{k+1}-\mathbf{G}_{k},\qquad k=1,\ldots,K-1, (3)

and denote the transition sequence by Δ​𝐆={Δ​𝐆k}k=1K−1\Delta\mathbf{G}=\{\Delta\mathbf{G}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K-1}. A lightweight transition predictor takes the current predictive state 𝐆k\mathbf{G}_{k} and estimates its subsequent latent change Δ​𝐆^k\widehat{\Delta\mathbf{G}}_{k}. We optimize

ℒtrans=1K−1​∑k=1K−1SmoothL1⁡(Δ​𝐆^k,sg⁡(Δ​𝐆k)).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{trans}}=\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K-1}\operatorname{SmoothL1}\left(\widehat{\Delta\mathbf{G}}_{k},\operatorname{sg}(\Delta\mathbf{G}_{k})\right). (4)

Predicting the residual transition rather than reconstructing another complete geometric state focuses this objective on how the latent scene configuration changes over time. Together with geometry reconstruction and masked representation prediction, transition prediction encourages 𝐆\mathbf{G} to capture both the spatial structure of the scene and its predictable temporal evolution.

Motor Representation Learning.

The predictive geometric representation is designed to retain a broad and structured account of scene geometry and its evolution. While such information is useful for predictive modeling, not every geometric variation is equally informative for control. In particular, Δ​𝐆\Delta\mathbf{G} may contain transitions induced by robot motion and object interaction together with variations that are only weakly related to the corresponding motor commands. We therefore use the geometric transitions as a motion-centric source and introduce action supervision to emphasize the component of these transitions that is informative for action generation. Specifically, a set of learnable motor queries cross-attends to the transition tokens in Δ​𝐆\Delta\mathbf{G}, which serve as keys and values. The resulting features form the motor representation 𝐙\mathbf{Z}. An action prediction head maps 𝐙\mathbf{Z} to a predicted action chunk 𝐀^\widehat{\mathbf{A}}, which is supervised by the ground-truth action chunk 𝐀\mathbf{A}:

ℒactpre=‖𝐀^−𝐀‖1.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}^{\mathrm{pre}}=\left\|\widehat{\mathbf{A}}-\mathbf{A}\right\|_{1}. (5)

The complete representation-pretraining objective is

ℒpre=ℒrec+λmask​ℒmask+λtrans​ℒtrans+ℒactpre,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pre}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{mask}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mask}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{trans}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{trans}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}^{\mathrm{pre}}, (6)

where λmask\lambda_{\mathrm{mask}} and λtrans\lambda_{\mathrm{trans}} balance the corresponding objectives.

3.2 Representation-Guided Policy Post-training

We next transfer the complementary information encoded by the predictive geometric and motor representations to a downstream policy. As shown in Fig.3, for each post-training example, the frozen pretrained model processes a multi-view training clip containing the current and future observations and extracts the target predictive geometric representation 𝐆\mathbf{G} and motor representation 𝐙\mathbf{Z}. These future-informed representations serve exclusively as privileged supervision, while the downstream policy continues to receive only its standard current-time inputs. Let OtO_{t} denote the current observation, ll the language instruction, and sts_{t} the robot state. The policy backbone processes (Ot,l,st)(O_{t},l,s_{t}) together with a set of learnable geometry queries. In addition to the intermediate features used by the policy for action generation, the geometry queries produce a sequence of predicted geometric representation 𝐆~={𝐆~k}k=1K\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}=\{\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}. We align these representations with the frozen targets 𝐆\mathbf{G} using

ℒgeo=1K​∑k=1KSmoothL1⁡(𝐆~k,sg⁡(𝐆k)),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geo}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\operatorname{SmoothL1}\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}_{k},\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{G}_{k})\right), (7)

which encourages the model to capture the current scene configuration together with its anticipated geometric evolution. The motor representation is transferred through a different interface, rather than requiring the policy to explicitly recover 𝐙\mathbf{Z} through an additional prediction output, we use 𝐙\mathbf{Z} as a guidance target for intermediate features along the action-generation pathway. Let 𝐙~\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}} denote the intermediate policy features, we align these features with the frozen motor representation target using a cosine-distance objective:

ℒalign=1−cos⁡(𝐙~,sg⁡(𝐙)).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}=1-\cos\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}},\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{Z})\right). (8)

Finally, we combine the two representation-guidance objectives with the native action-generation objective of the downstream policy:

ℒpost=ℒactpost+λgeo​ℒgeo+λalign​ℒalign,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{post}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}^{\mathrm{post}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{geo}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geo}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}, (9)

where ℒactpost\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}^{\mathrm{post}} denotes the action-generation objective of the policy backbone. The representation guidance therefore does not replace the backbone’s native action modeling objective, but complements it with predictive geometric and motor supervision. At inference time, neither future observations nor the pretrained representation model is required.

4 Experiment

We design our experiments to answer three questions:

  1. (Q1)

    Does CPR guidance improve downstream manipulation performance across diverse settings?

  2. (Q2)

    Does CPR generalize across policy paradigms while improving predictive modeling?

  3. (Q3)

    How should CPR be organized and transferred for effective policy learning?

Experimental setup.

We evaluate CPR guidance across simulated and real-world manipulation settings, covering task suites, robot embodiments, and downstream policies. Unless otherwise specified, we use QwenOFT (Yang et al., 2025a; Kim et al., 2025) as the downstream policy baseline and denote this baseline as Ours w/o CPR. Our evaluation includes LIBERO (Liu et al., 2024), LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025), SimplerEnv (Li et al., 2024b), and four real-world manipulation tasks. Our real-world evaluation consists of three bimanual tasks, remove a stopper, pick up tubes into box, and transfer liquid into an erlenmeyer, together with one single-arm task, make a burger. These tasks cover bimanual coordination, object transfer, liquid manipulation, and multi-stage manipulation, providing challenges for evaluating perception and action generation in physical environments. We compare against policy baselines without predictive-representation guidance, including OpenVLA-OFT (Kim et al., 2025) and π0\pi_{0} (Black et al., 2024). We further compare with input-centric approaches that incorporate geometric information into the policy input, including GeoVLA (Sun et al., 2025), 3D-CAVLA (Bhat et al., 2025), SpatialVLA (Qu et al., 2025), and FALCON (Zhang et al., 2025b). In addition, we include prediction-centric approaches that provide future or predictive information to policy learning, including 4D-WAM (Yang et al., 2026a), ELAN4D (He et al., 2026), QDepth-VLA (Li et al., 2025c), and WoG (Su et al., 2026). Implementation details and training configurations are provided in the Appendix.F and B.

4.1 (Q1): Simulation and Real-World Results

Simulation Results on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus.

We first evaluate CPR on manipulation and under distribution shifts using LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus. As shown in Tab. 2, CPR improves the average LIBERO success rate from 96.6% to 98.6%, an absolute gain of 2.0 percentage points, with notable improvements on the Spatial and Long suites. We further evaluate the policy zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus without adaptation, where CPR increases the overall task-count-weighted success rate from 75.0% to 81.7%. The gains on both benchmarks indicate that complementary predictive guidance benefits manipulation under both nominal and shifted environments, providing structured geometric information together with action-aware cues for downstream control.

Simulation Results on WidowX.

We next evaluate the method in SimplerEnv using the WidowX robot. As reported in Tab. 2, CPR guidance raises the average success rate from 61.5% to 71.9%, corresponding to an absolute gain of 10.4 percentage points. The improvement on Stack Cube is especially informative because successful stacking requires accurate reasoning about the relative configuration of the manipulated cube and its target, as well as coordinated actions as the scene evolves. The gain on this task is consistent with the intended roles of the two representations: predictive geometric guidance provides structured information about scene configuration and its evolution, while motor guidance emphasizes action-aware transitions associated with manipulation.

Real-world evaluation.

We evaluate CPR on four real-world manipulation tasks shown in Fig. 4. The CPR-guided model consistently outperforms the baselines across tasks. The improvements are particularly pronounced on fine-grained manipulation tasks, such as Remove Stopper and Transfer Liquid, where precise spatial reasoning and action execution are required. By providing fine-grained geometric perception together with predictive information about future states, CPR enables the policy to better anticipate object configurations and execute more precise interactions. These results demonstrate that the complementary predictive guidance learned by CPR translates from simulation to real-world manipulation, particularly in tasks requiring accurate and fine-grained control.

4.2 (Q2): Transfer Across Diverse Policy Paradigms

Transfer to Diverse VLA Models.

To examine whether CPR depends on a particular downstream policy architecture, we integrate the same representation guidance into two additional VLA models, GR00T-style (Bjorck et al., 2025) and π0\pi_{0}-style models (Black et al., 2024). The representation pretraining procedure and the roles of the two representations remain unchanged, while their transfer interfaces are adapted to the corresponding downstream architectures. As shown in Fig. 5, adding the same alignment objective improves the average success rate of GR00T from 62.5% to 74.0%. Similarly, π0\pi_{0} improves from 59.4% to 68.8%, corresponding to a gain of 9.4 percentage points. Together with the gains observed for OFT, these results indicate that the proposed guidance is compatible with substantially different VLA architectures and is not tied to a single action-generation mechanism.

Transfer to World Action Models.

We further investigate whether complementary predictive representations remain useful for the WAM paradigm. We integrate CPR into FastWAM (Yuan et al., 2026), which jointly models future world evolution and robot actions. To preserve the respective roles of the two representations, we introduce an additional geometry DiT branch in parallel with the original world and action modeling branches for predictive geometric modeling, while using the motor representation to provide action-aware guidance to the action branch. As shown in Tab. 3, incorporating CPR improves the average LIBERO success rate of FastWAM from 97.6% to 98.5%. Although FastWAM already explicitly models future world evolution, these results suggest that structured predictive geometry and action-aware guidance can provide complementary information beyond the original world-action modeling objective. Combined with the results across three VLA architectures, this experiment further demonstrates the broad compatibility of CPR across substantially different policies. More details are provided in the Appendix.C.2.

4.3 (Q3): Analysis of Representation Design and Transfer

Effect of Complementary Predictive Representation Guidance.

To examine complementary contributions of the two predictive representations, we conduct an ablation study on the WidowX evaluation, with results reported in Tab. 5. Variant (a) corresponds to the VLA baseline without representation guidance. Introducing the predictive geometric representation in variant (b) improves the average success rate from 61.5% to 66.7%, yielding a gain of 5.2%. Variant (c) instead transfers the motor representation by aligning it with the intermediate features used for action generation. This variant improves the average success rate to 67.7%, outperforming the baseline by 6.2%. This result supports motor representation in providing action-aware predictive guidance to the action-generation pathway. Finally, combining both representations in variant (d) achieves the best average success rate of 71.9%, corresponding to a 10.4% absolute improvement over the baseline. Combining predictive geometric and motor representation allows the downstream policy to benefit from predictive geometric information and action-aware dynamics, leading to the strongest performance.

Effect of Representation Organization.

We examine whether assigning predictive geometry and action-aware information to complementary representations is beneficial. In the unified variant, the motor branch is removed, and the predictive geometric representation is jointly supervised by the action objective and aligned with intermediate features of the downstream VLA. As shown in Tab. 5, the unified representation improves the average success rate from 61.5% to 67.7%, but remains below our complementary design at 71.9%, which indicates that providing complementary representations for structured predictive geometry and action-aware information is more effective than asking a single representation to serve both roles under training setup. To further probe encoded information, we evaluate the pretrained representations zero-shot on LIBERO-90(Liu et al., 2024). As shown in Fig. 6, the motor representation concentrates more samples in the low action-error region, while the predictive geometric representation better preserves scene structure in depth probing, where the pseudo labels are generated by DepthAnything(Lin et al., 2025). The latter recovers more faithful object geometry and relative depth relationships compared with the unified representation. Together, these results suggest that assigning distinct roles to predictive geometric and motor representations helps preserve both geometric fidelity and action-relevant information, supporting the complementary design of CPR. More details are provided in Appendix A.3.

5 Conclusion

We study complementary predictive representation learning to connect evolving scene geometry with action generation. A predictive geometric representation captures structured scene evolution, while a motor representation emphasizes action-relevant geometric transitions; the two are transferred to downstream policies through dedicated guidance pathways without requiring future observations at inference time. Experiments across simulated and real-world manipulation settings demonstrate consistent gains across VLA architectures and WAMs, including improvements in both manipulation performance and future world/action prediction. These results highlight the importance of organizing predictive geometric information according to its role in downstream control.
