APPENDIX CONTENTS

Appendix A Additional Experiments

A.1 (Q1): Simulation and Real-World Results

Full LIBERO-Plus Results.

We provide the detailed results on the seven perturbation types of LIBERO-Plus in Tab. 6, which provide a more detailed view of the robustness gains reported in the main experiments.

Real-World Out-of-Distribution Generalization.

We further evaluate the ability of CPR to generalize to unseen visual and spatial conditions without additional training. Starting from the same real-world tasks described above, we introduce task-specific perturbations that change the observation distribution while preserving the underlying manipulation objective. Specifically, as shown in Fig.8, for Remove Stopper, we shift the position of the erlenmeyer flask to alter the relative geometry between the two arms and the manipulated object. For Store Tubes, we randomly vary the height of the target box, requiring the policy to adapt to changes in the target geometry. For Transfer Liquid, we introduce a randomly moving toy car as a dynamic visual distractor during execution, increasing the difficulty of separating task-relevant objects from irrelevant scene motion. For Make a Burger, we add multiple irrelevant objects to the workspace, introducing additional visual clutter.

These perturbations respectively introduce changes in object placement, target geometry, dynamic visual context, and scene clutter, while keeping the underlying task semantics unchanged. As shown in Fig. 7, CPR achieves the highest success rate on all four tasks and improves the overall average success rate from 21.7% for the baseline without CPR to 50.0%. The consistent improvement under these unseen conditions suggests that complementary predictive representation guidance can provide useful geometric and action-aware information beyond the nominal training distribution, helping the downstream policy maintain effective manipulation behavior under changes in visual and spatial context.

A.2 (Q2): Transfer Across Diverse Policy Paradigms

Quantitative Analysis of FastWAM.

Beyond downstream task success in Sec.4.2, we examine whether CPR improves the predictive capabilities of WAMs themselves. We freeze the FastWAM models trained on LIBERO and evaluate them on LIBERO-90 without additional adaptation. Future visual prediction is evaluated using PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, while action prediction is measured by the ℓ1\ell_{1} error between predicted and ground-truth actions. As shown in Tab. 7, CPR consistently improves both future visual prediction and action prediction. PSNR increases from 19.67 to 22.91, SSIM improves from 0.764 to 0.803, and LPIPS decreases from 0.229 to 0.186. The action ℓ1\ell_{1} error decreases from 0.124 to 0.075, corresponding to a relative reduction of approximately 39.5%. These results provide evidence that the proposed representation guidance improves not only downstream manipulation performance but also the predictive quality of the underlying world-action model. The improvement in visual prediction is consistent with the structured geometric supervision provided by the predictive geometric representation, while the reduction in action error is consistent with the action-aware information emphasized by the motor representation. Together, they provide complementary predictive guidance for jointly modeling future world evolution and robot actions.

Qualitative Analysis of FastWAM.

We provide additional qualitative comparisons to further examine the improvements observed in the zero-shot world- and action-prediction evaluation on LIBERO-90. As illustrated in Fig. 10, the differences between FastWAM with and without CPR are evident in both geometric fidelity and action execution.

In Fig. 10(a), we consider a scene in which the robot is preparing to grasp a can. Without complementary predictive representation guidance, the predicted future frames exhibit a noticeable discrepancy in the estimated geometric configuration, particularly in the relative position between the gripper and the target object. As a consequence, the generated gripper trajectory does not reach the appropriate grasp location, resulting in an action prediction that is inconsistent with the target interaction. With CPR guidance, the predicted frames more accurately preserve the geometric configuration of the object and gripper, allowing the generated trajectory to approach the can at a more appropriate location. This qualitative example is consistent with the role of the predictive geometric representation in providing structured geometric information for future scene prediction. We observe similar differences in more temporally extended interactions, as shown in (b) and (c). Without CPR, the generated videos may exhibit missing or ambiguous object structures and progressively deviate from the expected scene evolution. At the same time, the predicted actions can become inconsistent with the intended manipulation sequence. For example, as shown in (c), in a drawer-opening interaction, the baseline predictions may fail to clearly represent the drawer’s changing configuration and do not adequately capture the corresponding opening motion. In contrast, FastWAM with CPR maintains more coherent object configurations over time and produces predictions that more faithfully reflect the evolving manipulation process.

These observations provide a qualitative counterpart to the quantitative improvements reported in Tab. 7. The predictive geometric representation encourages the model to preserve structured geometric information during future-world modeling, which can improve the fidelity of object shape, relative spatial configuration, and scene evolution in the generated frames. Meanwhile, the motor representation emphasizes action-aware information from geometric transitions, providing guidance that is more directly associated with the execution of the corresponding manipulation. The combination therefore allows the model to better maintain both the evolving geometric state of the scene and the action sequence associated with that evolution. Overall, the qualitative results suggest that CPR improves the consistency between predicted future geometry and predicted robot actions. Rather than improving only the visual appearance of individual future frames, the complementary guidance helps the model maintain a more coherent correspondence between what the scene is expected to become and what action should be taken as it evolves. This observation is consistent with the complementary roles of the predictive geometric and motor representations in our framework.

A.3 (Q3): Analysis of Representation Design and Transfer

More Details of Representation Organization.

We provide additional details of the representation-organization analysis reported in Sec. 4.3. For action probing, we visualize the number of samples falling into each ℓ1\ell_{1}-loss bin for the different representation variants. As shown in Fig. 11, the overlapping bar charts provide the full error distributions underlying the action-probing analysis in the main paper, offering a more detailed view of how each representation distributes across low- and high-error regions.

We further provide qualitative results for the depth-probing experiment. As shown in Fig. 13, the depth predictions obtained from the predictive geometric representation more faithfully recover the spatial structure of the corresponding scenes than those obtained from the unified representation. In particular, the predicted maps better preserve object boundaries, relative depth relationships, and major scene structures across the future frames. These qualitative observations complement the quantitative probing results and provide additional evidence that the predictive geometric representation retains richer geometric information than the unified representation.

Comparison with Predictive Representation Learning Methods.

Existing predictive representation learning methods differ in both their learned representations and downstream policy architectures, making direct comparisons potentially confounded by differences in the overall training pipeline. To isolate the effect of predictive representation learning, we therefore integrate several representative approaches into the same downstream VLA framework and evaluate them under a unified setting on the WidowX benchmark. As shown in Tab. 8, our method achieves the highest average success rate of 71.9%, compared with 64.6% for WoG (Su et al., 2026), 67.7% for FutureVLA (Xu et al., 2026), and 68.8% for RepWAM (Wang et al., 2026a). Since these methods are evaluated with the same downstream policy framework, the comparison provides a more controlled assessment of the predictive representations used to guide policy learning. The result suggests that the benefit of predictive guidance depends not only on exposing the policy to future information, but also on how that information is organized for downstream control. Our method provides structured predictive geometric information together with action-aware information extracted from geometric transitions, allowing these complementary signals to be transferred through dedicated supervision pathways.

Effect of Predictive Representation Pretraining Objectives.

We further examine the contribution of the three objectives used to learn the predictive geometric representation. Starting from the downstream baseline, introducing geometry reconstruction ℒrec\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}} together with the action-supervised motor branch improves the average success rate from 61.5% to 65.6%, indicating that preserving geometric structure already provides useful guidance for downstream control. Adding masked geometric state prediction ℒmask\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mask}} further increases the performance to 68.8%, suggesting that contextual prediction across temporal states helps the representation capture richer temporal dependencies. Finally, incorporating geometric transition prediction ℒtrans\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{trans}} yields the best result of 71.9%. This additional gain indicates that explicitly modeling transitions between consecutive geometric states provides further information about scene evolution that is useful for downstream action generation. Overall, the progressive improvements support the complementary roles of structural, contextual, and transition-level supervision in shaping the predictive geometric representation.

Qualitative Analysis of Visual Attention.

We also visualize the attention maps of the baseline and CPR-guided policies under the same observations and language instructions. As shown in Fig. 14, the baseline exhibits relatively diffuse attention, whereas the CPR-guided model more consistently concentrates on task-relevant objects, target regions, and surrounding spatial context. In particular, stronger localization is observed around manipulated objects and regions involved in the ongoing interaction. These qualitative observations are consistent with the intended roles of the two guidance signals: predictive geometric supervision encourages structured scene understanding, while motor guidance emphasizes information associated with action-aware transitions. Although attention maps do not directly measure policy reasoning, they provide qualitative evidence that CPR can encourage more task-focused visual representations.

Effect of Geometric Transitions for Motor Representation Learning.

We next examine why the motor representation is learned from geometric transitions rather than directly from predictive geometric states. We construct a variant in which the motion queries attend directly to 𝐆\mathbf{G} instead of Δ​𝐆\Delta\mathbf{G} while keeping the remaining training procedure unchanged. As shown in Tab. 10, directly using the predictive geometric states yields an average success rate of 68.8%, whereas using geometric transitions increases the performance to 71.9%, an absolute gain of 3.1 percentage points. This result supports the use of transitions as the input to motor representation learning. A possible interpretation is that consecutive predictive states share substantial information describing scene structure, whereas their difference emphasizes temporal variation. Using Δ​𝐆\Delta\mathbf{G} therefore provides a more action-oriented signal from which action supervision can identify information associated with motor commands.

Effect of the Motor Representation Alignment Layer.

We investigate where motor guidance should be introduced within the downstream VLA backbone. Specifically, we apply the same motor representation alignment objective to intermediate features from different transformer layers while keeping the remaining training configuration unchanged. As reported in Tab. 11, performance reaches its maximum at layer 12, with an average success rate of 71.9%. The performance decreases when the alignment point is moved toward deeper layers. This suggests that motor guidance is most effective at an intermediate stage of the policy representation, where the features have incorporated sufficient contextual information while retaining flexibility to influence subsequent action generation. Based on this result, we use layer 12 for motor representation alignment in the remaining experiments.

Effect of the Foundation Encoder.

We further examine the dependence of representation pretraining on the chosen foundation encoder. We compare DINO(Oquab et al., 2023), which provides generic visual representations, with VGGT(Wang et al., 2025), which provides stronger geometric structure. As shown in Tab. 12, both encoders lead to competitive downstream performance, achieving 69.8% and 71.9% average success rates, respectively. VGGT provides the stronger overall result and a notable advantage on Stack Cube, which requires reasoning about relative object geometry. At the same time, DINO remains competitive and performs better on Put Carrot and Put Eggplant. These results suggest that the proposed representation learning framework can utilize different pretrained feature spaces while benefiting from a foundation model with stronger geometric structure.

Effect of the Geometry-Guidance Weight.

We investigate the effect of the geometry-guidance loss weight λgeo\lambda_{\mathrm{geo}} in the downstream post-training objective on the WidowX evaluation. As shown in Tab. 13, the average success rate initially improves as the weight increases from 0.1 to 0.3, reaching the best performance of 71.9%. Further increasing λgeo\lambda_{\mathrm{geo}} leads to a gradual performance degradation. These results suggest that the predictive geometric supervision is most effective when its contribution is appropriately balanced with the native action-generation objective. A relatively small geometry-guidance weight may provide insufficient supervision for transferring the structured predictive geometric information, whereas overly strong geometric supervision may place excessive emphasis on representation matching and reduce the relative influence of the action-generation objective. We therefore set λgeo=0.3\lambda_{\mathrm{geo}}=0.3 in the remaining experiments.

Comparison of Guidance Paradigms.

To further examine the design of CPR, we compare our approach with two representative guidance paradigms under the same downstream VLA framework and training setting. The input-centric variant directly provides current-frame VGGT features to the policy, allowing it to access explicit geometric information from the observed scene. The prediction-centric variant instead uses future VGGT features as a predictive target for guidance. In contrast, our method learns a predictive geometric representation from dense geometric features and further extracts action-aware information from geometric transitions.

As shown in Tab. 14, the input-centric and prediction-centric variants achieve average success rates of 63.5% and 65.6%, respectively, while CPR reaches 71.9%. The consistent improvement suggests that explicitly incorporating current geometry or future geometric prediction alone does not fully capture the complementary information needed for action generation. By organizing predictive geometry together with action-aware information extracted from geometric transitions, CPR provides a more effective interface for downstream policy learning.

Qualitative Analysis of Predictive Geometry.

We further qualitatively examine whether the geometry-query pathway transfers meaningful predictive geometric information into the downstream policy. Following the protocol described in the main paper, we freeze the post-trained policy and extract its predicted geometry-query features from current-time inputs. A lightweight DPT-based depth probe (Ranftl et al., 2021) is then trained on these frozen features, while keeping the VLA backbone and the geometry-query representations fixed. Since ground-truth depth annotations are unavailable for the evaluated observations, we use pseudo-depth maps generated by Depth Anything (Lin et al., 2025) as supervision for the probe.

As illustrated in Fig. 16, we provide qualitative results on both LIBERO and real-world manipulation scenes. For the LIBERO examples, the geometry-query features recover major spatial structures across both the main and wrist views, including object boundaries, relative depth relationships, and scene layout. Similar behavior is observed in the real-world examples across the main view and the two wrist views, suggesting that the learned geometry-query pathway preserves meaningful spatial structure under different embodiments and visual configurations. Importantly, these geometric features are inferred solely from current-time inputs, while their predictive supervision during post-training is constructed from future-informed representations. The qualitative results therefore provide evidence that the geometry-query pathway transfers predictive geometric information into the downstream policy, rather than merely encoding the current visual appearance.

Appendix B Training Details

B.1 Datasets

For predictive representation pretraining, we construct a mixed training corpus that combines robot manipulation datasets with additional general-purpose data. The robot manipulation data are designed to provide diverse interaction trajectories with explicit visuomotor structure and action supervision. We organize these data into two broad groups. The first group consists primarily of conventional robot manipulation datasets, including Open X-Embodiment (OXE)(Collaboration, 2023), RoboTwin(Chen et al., 2025a), and LIBERO(exclude LIBERO-90)(Liu et al., 2024). These datasets provide diverse robotic interaction trajectories and action-labeled manipulation behaviors, which expose the representation model to a broad range of object interactions, robot motions, and action-conditioned scene changes. The second group consists of ego data, which provide substantially broader interaction diversity and complementary visuomotor observations beyond conventional fixed-base robot manipulation datasets(Jin et al., 2026; Grauman et al., 2022). In addition, we incorporate several general-purpose datasets(Goyal et al., 2017) to further increase the diversity of visual scenes and improve the model’s ability to capture geometric structure across a broader range of environments. We use the mixed corpus throughout representation pretraining rather than restricting individual training stages to a specific data source. This combination provides both manipulation-oriented action supervision and diverse visual-geometric observations, allowing the predictive representations to learn scene structure and its evolution from a broader distribution of interaction data.

B.2 Training Protocol

Pretraining Configurations.

We train the predictive representation model using a progressive multi-stage training protocol. Rather than introducing all objectives simultaneously, we gradually add the supervision objectives according to the role they play in shaping the complementary representations. This curriculum first establishes structurally informative geometric representations, then encourages temporal contextual modeling and transition prediction, and finally introduces action supervision to extract the motor representation.

1) Stage 1: Geometry Reconstruction. We first train the representation model using only the geometry reconstruction objective ℒrec\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}. At this stage, the mixed robot manipulation and general-purpose data are used to establish an initial predictive geometric representation. Since the representation is obtained through hierarchical tokenization and temporal compression, the reconstruction objective provides a direct signal for preserving the geometric information contained in the pretrained foundation features.

2) Stage 2: Masked Geometric Representation Prediction. After the representation acquires basic geometric structure, we introduce the masked geometric state prediction objective ℒmask\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mask}}. Masked temporal slots are inferred from the available contextual states, encouraging the model to capture dependencies across the interaction sequence. This stage improves the ability of the predictive geometric representation to infer missing geometric information from temporal context.

3) Stage 3: Geometric Transition Prediction. We next introduce the geometric transition prediction objective ℒtrans\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{trans}}. In this stage, the representation model is explicitly trained to predict changes between consecutive predictive geometric states. This encourages the learned representation not only to describe scene structure but also to capture how the geometric configuration evolves over time.

4) Stage 4: Motor Representation Learning. Finally, we introduce the action prediction objective ℒactpre\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}^{\mathrm{pre}} using conventional robot manipulation data that provide temporally aligned action supervision. Motion queries attend to the geometric transitions Δ​𝐆\Delta\mathbf{G}, and the resulting motor representation is supervised with the corresponding action chunks. This final stage extracts action-aware information from the learned geometric transitions and completes the learning of the complementary predictive geometric and motor representations.

Unless otherwise specified, each stage is initialized from the parameters obtained in the preceding stage. We set λmask=0.5\lambda_{\mathrm{mask}}=0.5, λtrans=0.5\lambda_{\mathrm{trans}}=0.5, and λvc=0.06\lambda_{\mathrm{vc}}=0.06. This progressive training strategy allows the model to first establish a structurally informative geometric representation before introducing increasingly task-oriented temporal and action supervision. We perform representation pretraining on 32 NVIDIA H200 GPUs with a global batch size of 512. The base learning rate is set to 1×10−51\times 10^{-5} with learning-rate decay, and the model is trained for a total of 120K optimization steps. The pretrained 3D foundation encoder remains frozen throughout representation pretraining.

Post-training Configurations.

For downstream post-training, the pretrained predictive representation model is kept frozen. For each training clip, it is used to construct the two privileged targets: the predictive geometric representation 𝐆\mathbf{G} and the motor representation 𝐙\mathbf{Z}. We initialize the downstream VLA visual-language backbone from Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2025a). The native action-generation objective of the corresponding VLA is retained throughout post-training, while the representation-guidance objectives are jointly optimized with it. We use a linear warm-up schedule for the first 5,000 optimization steps. To facilitate stable adaptation, we further apply a cosine decay schedule to the coefficient of the latent motor-alignment loss, λalign\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}, gradually reducing the strength of latent alignment supervision as training progresses. Importantly, the pretrained representation model is not used by the downstream policy at inference time. After post-training, the policy operates solely on its standard current-time inputs, with the predictive and motor representations serving only as privileged supervision during training.

Appendix C Model Details

C.1 Hierarchical Geometric Tokenization

We use a hierarchical tokenization process to convert dense multi-view video features extracted by VGGT (Wang et al., 2025) into a compact and temporally organized geometric token sequence. Given a multi-frame, multi-view input clip, each RGB image is first resized and padded following the input preprocessing procedure of VGGT, resulting in a resolution of 518×518518\times 518. The processed images are then independently fed into a frozen VGGT encoder to obtain dense geometric features for each frame-view pair. Since the number of available camera views varies across the pretraining datasets, we use a maximum of three input views at each time step. Samples with fewer than three views are zero-padded to the maximum view number, and the corresponding padded views are masked throughout the subsequent attention operations. After view-level compression, we further aggregate frame-level geometric states along the temporal dimension. Inspired by hierarchical temporal compression designs (Wan et al., 2025), we retain the first frame 𝐇0\mathbf{H}_{0} as an initial-observation anchor and group every four subsequent frames into a temporal slot. Specifically, for each temporal group, a set of learnable temporal queries performs cross-attention over the frame-level geometric features within the corresponding group. The frame features serve as keys and values, while the learnable temporal queries serve as queries. Learnable frame-position embeddings are added before temporal aggregation to preserve the relative temporal ordering of frames within each group. We further construct the temporal attention mask to match the grouping structure of the temporal slots. Frame features belonging to the same temporal group are mutually visible to the corresponding temporal queries, whereas features from different groups are prevented from attending to each other during this local aggregation stage. Within each temporal group, padded frame positions are additionally masked so that invalid frames do not affect the resulting representation. The first frame is treated as a dedicated temporal anchor and is retained without being merged with subsequent frames.

Through this hierarchical view- and time-wise compression, dense multi-view VGGT features are progressively transformed into a compact tokenized geometric sequence SS, where the first temporal slot corresponds to the initial observation and each subsequent slot summarizes a group of four consecutive frames. This hierarchical design substantially reduces the number of geometric tokens while preserving both view-specific information and temporal ordering. More importantly, the resulting sequence explicitly organizes geometric information at two levels: view aggregation captures a compact representation of the scene from multiple camera perspectives, while temporal aggregation provides a structured representation for modeling the evolution of scene geometry over the interaction sequence.

C.2 Details of FastWAM

FastWAM (Yuan et al., 2026) differs from conventional VLA models (Bjorck et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025; Black et al., 2024), in that it jointly models future visual observations and robot actions through a generative world-action architecture. We therefore introduce additional interfaces to incorporate the two complementary predictive representations into the original FastWAM architecture while preserving its native world- and action-generation mechanisms.

Specifically, FastWAM consists of a visual world modeling branch implemented with a WAN(Wan et al., 2025) and an action-generation branch. To incorporate the predictive geometric representation, we introduce an additional geometry branch with an architecture and initialization strategy analogous to the original action branch. The geometry branch is trained to model the predictive geometric representations provided by the pretrained representation model, and operates in parallel with the original world and action modeling branches. This enables FastWAM to receive explicit supervision on the structured evolution of scene geometry in addition to its original visual world-prediction objective. The motor representation is incorporated through the action-generation pathway. Rather than introducing an additional generative branch for the motor representation, we use the pretrained motor representation as a latent guidance target for intermediate features within the action branch. Specifically, the corresponding intermediate action features are aligned with the motor representation using the same representation-level alignment objective as in the VLA setting. This provides action-aware geometric information directly to the branch responsible for generating robot actions, while leaving the native action modeling objective of FastWAM unchanged.

Because the predictive geometric representation is organized into temporal slots, an additional temporal alignment mechanism is required to establish correspondence between the geometric representation and the visual tokens in FastWAM. We therefore introduce a structured attention mask that explicitly couples temporally corresponding video and geometry slots. As illustrated in Fig. 17, each video slot is allowed to attend to its corresponding geometry slot, enabling the visual representation at a given temporal position to access the geometric information associated with the same stage of the interaction. Conversely, each geometry slot is also allowed to attend to the corresponding video slot. This bidirectional local visibility establishes an explicit correspondence between visual and geometric representations while preventing a geometry slot from indiscriminately attending to temporally unrelated video tokens. The resulting attention pattern therefore encourages localized video-geometry interaction: Such slot-level correspondence allows the model to jointly reason about visual appearance and geometric structure at matched temporal positions, while preserving the temporal organization of the predictive representation. The mask is applied in addition to the native attention structure of FastWAM and does not require additional geometric observations at inference time. During inference, the additional geometry branch and the pretrained representation model are not required to receive externally provided geometric observations. The downstream FastWAM operates using its standard current-time visual input, from which the learned model generates the future world evolution and corresponding actions. Thus, as in the VLA setting, the predictive geometric and motor representations are used to provide privileged supervision during training, while no extra geometry input is required during deployment.

Appendix D Limitations and Future Work

Our current framework primarily focuses on visual geometry and its temporal evolution to construct predictive and action-aware representations. An interesting direction for future work is to further incorporate tactile information into the same representation-learning framework. Tactile observations provide complementary cues about contact states, interaction forces, and fine-grained object configurations that may not be fully observable from vision alone. Integrating visual geometry with tactile feedback could therefore provide a richer representation of scene evolution, particularly for contact-rich manipulation and interactions involving occlusion or subtle physical state changes. More broadly, exploring multimodal predictive representations that jointly capture visual, geometric, and tactile evolution may further strengthen the connection between world modeling and action generation.

Appendix E Simulation and Real-World Evaluation Details

E.1 Simulation Evaluation Details

We provide detailed descriptions of the simulation benchmarks employed in our experiments.

SimplerEnv Benchmark.

To assess cross-embodiment generalization and investigate the correlation between simulation performance and real-world performance, we conduct experiments on the SimplerEnv benchmark (Li et al., 2024b) using the WidowX robot.

For the WidowX robot, we use the Visual Matching setting to ensure consistency with the data distribution of the Bridge dataset(Ebert et al., 2021a). We evaluate the robot on four manipulation tasks: Put Carrot on Plate (Put Carrot), Put Spoon on Towel (Put Spoon), Stack Green on Yellow (Stack Cube), and Put Eggplant in Basket (Put Eggplant). All experiments on SimplerEnv strictly follow the standard evaluation protocol established by CogAct (Li et al., 2024a).

LIBERO Benchmark.

We additionally evaluate our method on the LIBERO benchmark (Liu et al., 2024) to examine different dimensions of temporal reasoning and knowledge transfer. In particular, we consider four task suites: Spatial, which evaluates spatial reasoning under different object configurations; Object, which focuses on object-centric manipulation involving diverse object categories; Goal, which evaluates goal-conditioned instruction following in static environments; and Long, which targets long-horizon planning over multi-stage manipulation tasks. Each suite consists of 10 tasks, and each task is provided with 50 human-teleoperated demonstrations.

LIBERO-Plus Benchmark.

LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025) evaluates the robustness of policies trained on LIBERO under controlled perturbations at test time. It introduces variations across seven dimensions: Camera Viewpoints, Robot Initial States, Language Instructions, Light Conditions, Background Textures, Sensor Noise, and Object Layouts. These perturbations are categorized into five difficulty levels, resulting in a total of 10,030 evaluation instances. We directly evaluate the checkpoint trained on LIBERO without performing any adaptation to the LIBERO-Plus perturbations. This evaluation protocol is designed to examine whether the learned policy representations remain effective when the observation distribution, robot initialization, or instruction formulation differs from those encountered during training.

E.2 Real-World Robot Evaluation Details

Real-World Robot Setup.

We conduct real-world experiments on both bimanual and single-arm manipulation platforms to evaluate the proposed CPR guidance under different embodiments and interaction requirements, as shown in Fig.18. For the bimanual setting, we use dual Flexiv robotic arms, each equipped with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper. Visual observations are captured using three Intel RealSense D435i RGB-D cameras, including two wrist-mounted cameras and one head-mounted camera. The combination of third-person and wrist-view observations provides complementary global and local views of the manipulation scene, which is particularly important for bimanual tasks involving object coordination and fine-grained manipulation.

For the single-arm setting, we use a Franka Research 3 robotic platform, equipped with a 7-DoF manipulator and joint-level torque and force sensing. Visual observations are obtained from an Intel RealSense D435i RGB-D camera mounted in an eye-on-base configuration, providing a global view of the manipulation workspace. We additionally mount a second RealSense camera on the robot wrist to provide close-up observations of the manipulated objects and end-effector interaction. The robot is equipped with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper for end-effector manipulation. These multi-view configurations provide both scene-level spatial context and fine-grained object-interaction cues for downstream action generation.

Baseline Models.

We compare our method with representative VLA baselines using different pretrained visual-language backbones. OpenVLA(Kim et al., 2024) is initialized from the publicly released checkpoint pretrained on the OXE(Collaboration, 2023) dataset. For our real-world experiments, we extend the original input interface to jointly process third-person and wrist-view images. We also evaluate π0\pi_{0}(Black et al., 2024), initialized from the official JAX checkpoint pretrained on the DROID(Khazatsky et al., 2024) dataset. Unless otherwise specified, the same downstream training protocol is used when incorporating CPR into the corresponding baseline model.

Real-World Task Suites.

As shown in Fig.19, we evaluate four real-world manipulation tasks covering bimanual coordination, geometric perception, contact-sensitive manipulation, and long-horizon task execution. The first three tasks are performed with the bimanual Flexiv setup, while the final task is conducted using the single-arm Franka platform.

  • •

    Remove a Stopper. The robot removes a stopper from an erlenmeyer flask and places it at a designated holder. The task first requires the left arm to grasp and stabilize the flask, after which the right arm grasps the stopper and places it accurately into the corresponding circular opening on the storage rack. Successful execution therefore requires precise relative positioning between the two arms and the manipulated objects, as well as coordinated bimanual actions during the stopper removal and placement stages.

  • •

    Pick up Tubes into Box. The robot sequentially transfers two tubes into a blue box using both arms. The left arm first grasps the brown tube and places it into the box, followed by the right arm grasping the blue tube and placing it into the corresponding location. The task requires accurate perception of object locations and target geometry, together with appropriate end-effector positioning for grasping and insertion. Since the two manipulation stages involve different objects and hand-object configurations, the policy must maintain consistent spatial grounding throughout the sequential execution.

  • •

    Transfer Liquid into an Erlenmeyer. The robot transfers liquid from a graduated cylinder into an erlenmeyer flask using a funnel. The right arm first grasps the funnel and inserts it into the flask with sufficient spatial precision. It then grasps the liquid-filled graduated cylinder and carefully tilts it to pour the liquid through the funnel. After the transfer, the right arm stabilizes the flask while the left arm removes the funnel and returns it to a designated holder on the rack. This task combines fine-grained geometric alignment, coordinated bimanual manipulation, sequential object-role changes, and long-horizon execution, making the relative spatial configuration of the objects and tools important throughout the interaction.

  • •

    Toast Breads and Make a Burger. This task is performed on the single-arm Franka platform and involves a longer sequence of manipulation stages. The robot first places two slices of bread into the toaster, then transfers one slice onto a plate. It subsequently grasps a meat patty from the rack and stacks it onto the bread, before placing the remaining bread slice on top to complete the burger. The task requires maintaining the correct object order and intermediate states across multiple manipulation stages, while accurately positioning each object for grasping, placement, and stacking.

Real-World Data Collection.

For downstream post-training, we collect 100 demonstrations for each of the three bimanual tasks and 60 demonstrations for the single-arm task. The collected trajectories are used to train the downstream policies.

Appendix F Details of Compared Methods

We compare our approach with representative methods from three groups: standard policy baselines, input-centric methods, and prediction-centric methods. This categorization distinguishes how geometric or predictive information is introduced into policy learning: standard policies rely primarily on the model’s native visual-language-action inputs, input-centric methods explicitly augment the current observation with geometric or spatial information, while prediction-centric methods introduce additional predictive or auxiliary supervision to encourage the policy to learn future, temporal, or geometric structure.

Standard Policy Baselines.

These methods generate robot actions from visual observations, language instructions, and, when applicable, proprioceptive states, without introducing an explicit future-representation or auxiliary geometric prediction target.

  • •

    OpenVLA-OFT(Kim et al., 2025). OpenVLA-OFT (Kim et al., 2025) is an optimized post-training recipe for OpenVLA(Kim et al., 2024) that studies action representations, decoding strategies, and fine-tuning objectives. Its policy uses continuous action representations together with action chunking, parallel decoding, and an ℓ1\ell_{1} regression objective for efficient multi-step action prediction. These design choices provide a strong and efficient baseline for adapting pretrained VLA models to downstream manipulation tasks.

  • •

    π0\pi_{0}(Black et al., 2024). π0\pi_{0} is a general-purpose VLA that augments a pretrained vision-language model with a dedicated action expert. The action expert generates continuous action chunks using conditional flow matching, allowing the model to produce smooth, high-frequency robot trajectories across multiple embodiments. The model is pretrained on diverse multi-robot manipulation data and subsequently adapted to downstream tasks through post-training.

Input-Centric Methods.

Input-centric methods enhance the policy primarily by providing additional geometric or spatial information derived from the current observation. Rather than constructing a predictive target from future observations, these approaches enrich the policy’s current-time spatial representation through depth, point clouds, geometric embeddings, or spatially structured tokens.

  • •

    GeoVLA(Sun et al., 2025). GeoVLA augments a VLA with explicit 3D geometric information derived from depth observations. Depth maps are converted into point clouds and processed by a dedicated Point Embedding Network to obtain 3D geometric embeddings. These embeddings are combined with the vision-language representation and processed by a 3D-enhanced action expert, providing the policy with explicit spatial information for action generation.

  • •

    3D-CAVLA (Bhat et al., 2025). 3D-CAVLA enhances VLA spatial awareness by incorporating depth perception and task-oriented visual context. The framework combines depth information with chain-of-thought reasoning and region-of-interest detection to focus the policy on task-relevant objects and spatial relationships. Its goal is to improve scene-context understanding and generalization to unseen manipulation tasks.

  • •

    SpatialVLA (Qu et al., 2025). SpatialVLA explicitly introduces spatial representations into a generalist robot policy through Ego3D Position Encoding, which injects 3D positional information into the visual representation. It further uses Adaptive Action Grids to represent spatial robot movements in a discretized and robot-adaptive action space, facilitating spatially grounded manipulation and transfer across robot setups.

  • •

    FALCON (Zhang et al., 2025b). FALCON injects spatially rich tokens into the action-generation pathway of a VLA through an Embodied Spatial Model and a Spatial-Enhanced Action Head. The spatial branch can use RGB input alone and can additionally incorporate geometric modalities such as depth or camera pose when available. By consuming spatial tokens directly at the action head rather than concatenating them into the vision-language backbone, FALCON aims to strengthen 3D spatial understanding while preserving the semantic representation of the VLA.

Prediction-Centric Methods.

Prediction-centric methods introduce additional predictive or temporally structured supervision during policy learning. Rather than only enriching the current observation, these approaches encourage the policy to capture future scene evolution, depth structure, robot motion, or other predictive information that can support action generation.

  • •

    4D-WAM (Yang et al., 2026a). 4D-WAM introduces spatiotemporal supervision into World Action Models using 3D trajectory fields. It employs motion alignment to encourage consistency of feature changes across adjacent frames and destination alignment to guide the model toward long-horizon target information. These objectives provide local motion and long-range destination supervision through representation alignment, without requiring additional geometric inputs at inference time.

  • •

    ELAN4D (He et al., 2026). ELAN4D provides embodiment-centric 4D supervision to VLA policies through future robot keypoint tracks. The tracks are derived from proprioceptive states using forward kinematics and describe the 3D displacement of robot joints and end-effectors over time. A lightweight auxiliary track decoder injects this predictive spatiotemporal supervision into the action-generation pathway during training, while the auxiliary branch can be removed at inference time.

  • •

    QDepth-VLA (Li et al., 2025c). QDepth-VLA introduces depth prediction as an auxiliary supervision task for VLA training. A dedicated depth expert predicts quantized latent depth tokens obtained from a VQ-VAE representation of depth maps, encouraging the policy to learn depth-aware features that capture geometric structure relevant to manipulation. Unlike methods that directly provide depth as an additional input, QDepth-VLA uses depth prediction to shape the learned representation through auxiliary supervision.

  • •

    WoG (Su et al., 2026). World Guidance (WoG) maps future observations into compact condition representations and uses them to guide action generation. The VLA is trained to jointly predict the compressed future condition and the corresponding action trajectory, introducing future-world modeling supervision in a compact condition space rather than requiring full future-image reconstruction. This design aims to retain predictive information that is useful for action generation while keeping the prediction target compact.

  • •

    WorldVLA (Cen et al., 2025). WorldVLA integrates visual world modeling and action generation within a unified autoregressive framework. The world model predicts future visual observations conditioned on the current scene and actions, while the action model predicts subsequent actions from visual observations. The two components are jointly trained so that future-world modeling and action generation provide mutual supervision. WorldVLA further introduces selective attention masking to reduce error propagation from previously generated actions during autoregressive action prediction.
